# Design mocks

New directions get tried as mocks before they touch the site: self-contained HTML pages in `mocks/` that Truman can open and use. The folder is gitignored, as are the prep scripts in `scripts-local/`, so mocks never deploy and this public repo never sees them. Since 2026-11-12 both folders sync between his PCs through a private repo, `TrumanBrown/photography-website-local`, whose git directory sits beside the checkout (`~/projects/photography-website-local.git`) and uses it as its work tree. His copilot-home hook pulls them when a session starts in the main checkout and commits and pushes them when a turn ends, so just work in `mocks/` as usual. Run git on them with `bash ~/.copilot/home-sync/photo-local.sh git <args>`; plain `git` talks to the public repo. Worktrees don't get them. Setup and conflicts: [docs/session-handoff.md](../../../docs/session-handoff.md#7-mocks-and-scripts-local). The house look they should start from is in [site-design.instructions.md](../../instructions/site-design.instructions.md) and the words in [site-copy.instructions.md](../../instructions/site-copy.instructions.md). Card art comes from the [stipple-plates](../stipple-plates/SKILL.md) skill, never from drawn icons.

## Truman's spec for a mock

- **A mock is the real experience without the real plumbing**: one file "I can open in a browser and actually use", real-looking data, empty, loading and error states, and good enough that someone shown it for ten seconds would think it was the finished feature. His reaction to text sketches: "these mocs are horrible, unusuable. I want actual mocks of what the end user experience would be" (2026-09-27).
- **Not default AI.** "NOT DEFAULT AI looking. This is so important... People automatically ignore websites if they have this" (2026-10-06). The list below is the spec.
- **Unique and useful.** "this is good but not unique, its the same idea as kriliion... inatguesser was unique and good" (2026-10-08). "are these really ones people would come back to?" (2026-09-28).
- **A flagship needn't be a game or about nature.** "it needs to be unique, solves an interesting use case, and a clean, profession UX. more fleshed out than the mini games" (2026-09-28), and it "isn't super basic like some of the hobbies we have done". Geography is an interest the site doesn't show yet. Ones he points to: iNatGuessr, The Pudding's 3D city, Krillion, and Magnitudle's "Size it up" ("people will come back to and it is learning as well").
- **Not held back by Azure cost.** Scope the idea at its best; the credit covers it (azure-ops).
- **Simple.** The first redesign round was "far too complicated, too much going on in the screen" (2026-10-06).
- **Portfolio looks must suit every session**, not only wildlife: "it's not just field photography, it's landscapes, cities, etc" (2026-10-06).
- **Desktop and a true phone view** in every mock, visible without resizing the window.
- **Built from the current site**: "remember to buidl it from the current ux not the old" (2026-10-08).
- **Some motion, not overboard**; the scroll-reveal era is over.

### The banned default-AI signature

From his 2026-10-06 brief. If a direction needs one of these, justify it in writing.

- Colour and surface: indigo-to-violet or blue-to-cyan gradients, gradient-filled headlines, glass (backdrop blur with faint white borders), a slate-900 dark mode with one glowing accent, blurred gradient blobs behind a hero, dot-grid, faint-grid or noise overlays, and opacity steps (`/80`, `/60`, `/40`) as the only contrast tool.
- Layout: the centred hero with a pill badge, a huge headline, a one-line subhead and two buttons; three-column feature grids of tinted rounded icons; bento grids; the same wide section with an eyebrow, heading, subhead and three cards repeated down the page; a testimonial or call-to-action band at the bottom.
- Detail: one big rounded radius and a large shadow on everything; cards that lift or grow on hover; bold tight Inter or Geist for every heading; emoji in headings; sparkle and rocket icons; staggered fade-up on scroll; canvas or map text in bold system fonts, and dashboard maps with glowing heat blobs.
- Copy: "Elevate", "Seamlessly", "Crafted with care", "Discover", "Journey", "Dive into".

## Run a round

1. If he asks, rewrite his prompt first and hand it back for him to edit (he did this on 2026-09-27 and 2026-10-06), with the banned list, the deliverables, the checks, and "state assumptions and keep working". Ask clarifying questions before writing it, hand back only the prompt and stop: "you're supposed to give me the refined prompt that I Will pass back to you... not immediately do the actual work" (2026-09-27). Ask again when he sends it back.
2. Read the real site first (pages, components, tokens, copy rules, content) and write a five-to-eight-point critique of what's there. The critique drives the directions.
3. Build in `mocks/<topic>/` and never touch `src/`. An `index.html` links each direction with a one-paragraph thesis and what it refuses. Use real content (session titles and photos, hobby JSON) and copy that follows the copy rules. Give every mock a desktop and phone toggle and a dark mode.
4. Directions that should diverge get their own CSS. Mocks meant to look like the live site copy the tokens from `src/styles/global.css` and self-host Libre Franklin, as `mocks/things-to-try/mock.css` does. Game mocks make no network calls: data comes from `scripts-local/prep-*.mjs` and assets are inlined.
5. For each direction, say what it took from where, what it left out, and the trade-off. End with two or three decisions for him and your recommendation. In a brainstorm, add "a much much longer list of less / to no mocks but technically feasible other ideas" (2026-09-28), and for each top idea a 1-to-10 confidence that you can build it, naming any external data, new service, key, rate limit, licence or re-architecture it needs.
6. Check it yourself: serve it, open every page, no console errors or failed requests, screenshots at desktop and phone width, and a reread against the banned list naming anything that slipped through.
7. Present it the way he can open it from Windows: `cd mocks && python3 -m http.server <free port> --bind 127.0.0.1` as a background service, then `http://localhost:<port>/<path>` links, plus the `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\...` path as a fallback (ship-and-ci). Keep earlier rounds collapsed at the bottom of the index.
8. Iterate on his verdicts. When he approves one, port it into `src/` ("port the look, not the mock's file structure"); helpers working in parallel should each own separate files. From there the normal ship rules apply.

## Hard-won lessons

1. **Text isn't a mock.** Describing an experience got "horrible, unusuable"; a working page gets real feedback.
2. **The first frame can give the game away.** A puzzle image animated in from its untransformed state and showed the full answer for a moment. Set the start state before first paint.
3. **Old styles make old-looking mocks.** Mocks built on the original `mocks/shell.css` drew "build it from the current ux". Copy today's tokens.
4. **Drawn icons failed three rounds.** Stipple plates from his own photos worked the first time.
5. **One idea per screen.** Every first-round direction tried to show too much; what he kept were single strong pieces from several directions.
6. **A copy of a good idea is still a copy.** Unique matters more to him than polish.
7. **Say when a request contradicts an earlier verdict.** He rejected the card-photo-becomes-header idea in mock F, later asked for a cover zoom, and rejected that once he saw it.
8. **A layout round can end with "keep it, but adjust".** Front door round 2 offered three ways to fill a page's blank space; he kept the plain one and asked for sizes instead (wider rail, centered column, bigger text, smaller pictures). Always include today's layout with only the fixes as a direction, and offer the sizing knobs (rail width, column width) as toggles.
9. **Explain every option in plain words.** Icon round 1 named its marks by jargon ("trig point") and got "i dont really understand them". Each option needs what it is, where it comes from on his site, and how it looks at its real size, shown where it will live (a tab strip, a search result, a home screen).
10. **A photo can't be the scene of a find-it toy.** Tide pooling round 1's best-liked direction used real pools from the Olympic coast as the scene and tapped into them. Each photo held organisms the toy didn't know: an orange crust and urchin spines said "Just rock". Outlining all life in five pools, by model and by hand, still mislabelled things, and animals cut from other photos and pasted in floated, a fish in open water with nothing under it (2026-11-16). Build the scene from parts instead, surfaces from CC0 scans and every organism placed on purpose, so a tap can't land on something unknown, and put each animal only where it would sit, resting on its shadow, at its size against the rest.
11. **A showpiece in the house look read as unfinished.** Welcome page round 1 kept most directions in ink and paper, with small type, white space, label blocks and slow page changes, and he called it "nowhere near final product" (2026-11-18). A front door should do what his reference did: one huge image with the parts laid over it, him standing in the scene, big coloured buttons that press, and motion that answers within a tenth of a second. Start a showpiece round at the boldness of the reference he gave, and film every interaction frame by frame before showing it (`scripts-local/mock-qa/`). A still screenshot hid that round 1's title screen sat frozen for a third of a second after its menu vanished.
12. **Parts laid over a photo take their colours from it.** Round 2's title screen put amber, green and blue keys, a pixel name, a dark role label and Libre Franklin counts over a blue mountain photo, and he said "I don't think (1) is a very consistent theme. the colors look kind of out of place, the spacing is weird" (2026-11-19). Over a full-bleed photo, draw the palette from the photo itself, keep one type family or two clearly distinct ones, and space everything on one grid.
13. **Anything alive in a scene has to move like it.** The round 2 osprey was a photo cutout sliding across the sky in a straight line, and "it looks slopppy like that just being dragged across" (2026-11-19). A creature needs its own motion (wingbeats, glides, banking into a curve, its own depth behind the right things) or it should stay out.
14. **Film motion on the real GPU, on a second load.** In welcome round 3, WSL's software WebGL starved the screencast (23 frames in 2.3 s), so a working entrance looked frozen in its strip. Windows Edge headless on his GPU films at 60 fps (`scripts-local/mock-qa/film-win.mjs` with `strip-json.mjs`, wrapped by `film-w.sh`). A fresh headless profile also compiles the GPU's effects on its first draw, an 80 to 180 ms hitch his everyday browser doesn't have, so `film-w.sh` loads the page once before filming, and `probe-stall.mjs` measures stalls in the page before anything gets "fixed". A warm-up that drew the UI at 0.2% opacity changed nothing.
15. **A picture that grows into the next page lands where that page shows it.** Round 3's dock grew its Mount Baker preview to full screen and then cut to an archive that opened on a sunset, the cut he rejected on 2026-10-16. `welcome-dest2.mjs` screenshots the live pages, opens the archive on a chosen photo with the site's own `lead-handover` note, and records where each landing target sits. The kit's `R3.land` then flies the picture into the archive's lead photo, the hobby card's drawing or the rail portrait, and the page fades in around it. A picture with nowhere to land gets the plain glass sheet instead.
16. **Test arrival on a slow line.** On localhost everything lands at once. Throttled to 4 Mbps (`THROTTLE` in the film tools, `slow-gate.mjs`), round 3's smaller cutout of him arrived before the photo and stood on bare blue sky for 300 ms, and the dock's preview showed as an empty glass box. Anything laid over the photo waits for the photo to decode, and anything with a picture in it waits for that picture, capped at 350 ms so a slow image never holds the page.
17. **A mock that fits a name to a photo must still show the photo on a wide screen.** Four of the five round 3 directions zoomed the arms-up photo in to make his name fill the width. A 3:2 photo covering a 2.8:1 window already loses its bottom half, so on his 3440 x 1440 monitor the zoom left sky, the name and his arms, and he couldn't see the mountains (2026-11-19). Every check had run at 1440 x 900 and 390 x 844. The kit now owns the limit: no direction may zoom past the point where the mountains' foot (`R3.SHOW_TO`, 66% of the photo's height) is on screen, and wider than about 3:1 the photo stops covering the width and its own edges carry on softly beside it (`scripts-local/prep-welcome-r3-wide.py`). The photo also needs a size as wide as the biggest screen it fills (3,840 px for 21:9). Check every full-screen mock at 21:9 (including 3440 x 1230, his monitor with the browser open) and 32:9 too, with `scripts-local/mock-qa/wide-check.mjs`, and compare against the old behaviour with `before-after.mjs`.
18. **The strip a depth effect uncovers is part of the picture.** Round 3's plate filled the space behind him by copying each row of the photo across from its farther side. At rest his cutout covers that fill, so every screenshot and film looked right, but with the pointer at one side the motion uncovered it: blue blocks beside his neck and a flat bar of mountain beside the summit, which he circled on his monitor (2026-11-20). The plate is now filled with OpenCV's Navier-Stokes inpainting, which carries the sky and the peak's edges in from around him (`scripts-local/prep-welcome-r3.py`). Mirroring the photo across his outline was worse: it grew a second summit. `scripts-local/sim-welcome-r3-reveal.py` draws the scene moved to its edges at monitor strength, and at phone strength with `PHONE=1` (a phone uncovers about twice as much of the photo), in under 2 s, so a fill can be judged before a browser runs. Check any depth effect with the pointer pinned at each edge and corner (`mock-qa/reveal-check.mjs`), not only at rest.
19. **A bird seen from behind reads as flying backwards.** Round 3's osprey was a drawn 3D puppet flying away from the viewer. From behind its outline is the same coming or going, so as it shrank and drifted he saw it "flying in the wrong direction" (2026-11-20). Fly a creature side-on, or a little from below, facing the way it moves, and take its motion from real footage instead of drawing it: `scripts-local/prep-welcome-bird.py` cuts one wingbeat and a glide frame from public-domain US Fish and Wildlife Service video of a bald eagle, fits the sky as a smooth colour field, separates the bird from it against the bird's own colours (so a motion-blurred wing stays soft without a blue edge) and lines every frame up on the white head and tail. Check the clip plays at real speed before using it: its other beats repeat every 8.5 frames at 24 fps, about 2.7 a second, which is right for a bald eagle. A tracking camera's tilt moves the bird far more than its own bob, so the bob comes from the wing motion. A pixel version only works on the page's own pixel grid and colours (C's slate and snow, half the name's font pixel). At its photo-real size it was a jagged speck that lost its white head. Keep it from flying behind controls: on a phone read the open sky between the top controls and the name from the layout, and on a desktop keep its body under the name. Check it close up over the real scene with `mock-qa/bird-follow.mjs`, its frame times on the GPU with `bird-smooth.mjs`, and Off and reduced motion with `bird-off.mjs`. No osprey clip showed one flapping side-on against clear sky. Wikimedia answers bulk downloads with HTTP 429, so send a descriptive User-Agent and pause between files.
20. **Real wingbeats on a ruler-straight path still look fake.** The eagle's frames came from footage, but it crossed at one height, and he asked for it to "dip ever so slightly and raise like birds do, not in a perfect line" (2026-11-20). Eagles cruise by flap-gliding: a few beats, then a glide that sinks about 3 to 4 degrees, then beats that climb back. `mocks/welcome/r3-bird.js` now does that: a glide sinks at 0.9 body lengths a second and the beats climb at 0.55, with the change eased over 0.28 s so the top and bottom of each dip are round, about one body length deep. It flaps again early if it sinks too far, glides only once it's back near its line, and its nose follows the slope. The per-beat body bob is 1.7 times what the footage gives, because at 40 px the true bob doesn't show. A wave of 2 px looked straight, so check the depth: `mock-qa/bird-trail.mjs` stamps a whole crossing into one picture, like Marey's chronophotographs, with `BEFORE=<old engine>` to compare.
21. **At sprite size the face has to be drawn by hand.** Cut from the footage at 9 px tail to head, the pixel eagle's head was two or three white pixels whose shape changed with the motion blur, and he said "the head is kind of hard to tell what it is" (2026-11-20). Pixel artists hand-place the one read that matters and leave the rest. `scripts-local/prep-welcome-bird.py` stamps a 5-row head (white head and neck, a slate eye, the yellow hooked beak) onto every frame at the head's place in the footage, which never moves because the frames are aligned on it, and the grid went from 9 to 11 px. Judge a head at its real size on the real sky (3 px a pixel on C at 1440), not only blown up: two of the five heads tried looked fine at 8x and read as a stuck-on blob at size.
22. **A preview at rest reads as a bug.** Round 3's dock opened with its preview lifted over the dock and the focus cards with their first card raised, the way tvOS shows focus, and A, C and D rested their cursor on Photographs. He saw a preview "when i am not hovering my cursor over it" (2026-11-20). On a page a mouse drives, nothing looks selected until the mouse is on it or the keyboard is. `R3.menu`'s `rest` option in `mocks/welcome/r3-kit.js` clears the selection when the mouse leaves the menu's box or the focus leaves its items, keeps it while the keyboard has an item, and waits while a door's sheet covers the page. An entrance that fades in a cursor with `fill: "backwards"` flashes it once nothing is selected, so drop those keyframes with the initial selection. `scripts-local/mock-qa/rest-check.mjs` walks each direction through rest, hover, away and the info button and records what shows at each step.
23. **A small door tile needs a mark, not a drawing or a portrait.** A 40 px stipple plate on a notification was "dot slop", and a photo of him on the Work door was out: "use a clean logo of work or related, like how the github has a good logo clean to it" (2026-11-20). This narrows lesson 4 for tiles: under about 120 px a door gets one solid mark (Phosphor Icons and Fluent Emoji, both MIT, collected by `scripts-local/prep-welcome-marks.py` into `mocks/welcome/assets/r3/marks.js`), and a plate shows only where it has room, whole: a close crop of a plate's dots looked like slop on a 200 px card too. His own crab traced from the tide pooling plate closed into a blob at 40 px, because the plate is a front view, so the crab mark is Fluent's top-down one. Microsoft's logos and product icons can't be used without a licence (its Trademark and Brand Guidelines), so Work is a plain briefcase. Judge marks at their real sizes over the real photo (`mock-qa/marks-check.mjs`, `marks-cands.mjs`).
24. **A tip that holds a link is a toggletip.** He asked for "a little info bubble... to link directly to the session and image that it is using" (2026-11-20). A tooltip can't hold a link: it closes as the pointer travels to it and the keyboard can't reach it. `R3.info` is a button with `aria-expanded` and a `popover` card right after it in the tab order. A resting mouse opens it after 160 ms, a 240 ms bridge keeps it open while the pointer crosses to the card, a click or tap pins it, and Escape or a press elsewhere closes it. It sits with the page's own chips at their height, and its link opens the session with the photo up (`#photo-6`: the lightbox counts the gallery grid, not the banner).
25. **When the person in the photo is small, the land comes over the name.** On the tarn photo he's about 50 by 160 px at 2,560, too small to cross a name the way his hands did in round 3. The summit does it instead. The name sits in the sky just in front of it (`R3.NEAR.name` 0.12, with the farthest land at 0.35 after the depth remap), the summit rises into the gap between Truman and Brown and covers the inner feet of the n and the B by 0.1 em (`?bite=0` keeps the letters whole), and the pointer slides it across the gap. `fitName` in `mocks/welcome/r4-title.js` fits the name against the land's outline on screen, row by row. A rock spire on the summit's flank counted as other land and shrank the name, so all land within the gap's width of the apex now counts as the summit (`rise()`). On desktops the name is at most 18.5% of the window's height, so the summit keeps its room.
26. **Cut masks come from the full-size split, decoded before they're needed.** Depth Anything V2 gives the sky a depth of exactly 0, but also pockets of far haze inside the land, so the sky is only the zero region that touches the top edge, and a 15 px band along the skyline is decided by colour unmixing (`scripts-local/prep-welcome-r4.py`). The mask the eagle flies behind was first made at the model's 1,280 px, which averaged the thin tree tops away, and on 21:9 the eagle drew over them. It's now the split's full-size alpha times the depth's choice of near land, saved at 2,560 px, and `mock-qa/r4-nearmask.mjs` tints it magenta over the scene to check. Drawn straight from an `<img>`, that bigger mask decoded during the eagle's first cut and dropped a frame on his GPU (`mock-qa/raf-where.mjs` placed it 70 ms after the eagle appeared). The kit now turns it into an `ImageBitmap` as it loads, off the main thread.
27. **How much of the photo must show decides where the soft sides start, so check his real browser size.** Round 3's photo went soft-sided past about 3:1. The tarn photo needs 61.5% of its height, from the sky over the name down to the reflection, which moved that point to 2.44:1, so 3440 x 1230, his 21:9 monitor with the browser open, got the soft frame. Centring the summit, which sits left of the photo's middle, then left 400 px of blur on the left and 40 on the right. Every check had run at 3440 x 1440. Now a wide window gives up sky first (its top down to 18% of the photo), then the reflection (its bottom up to 70%), before the sides go soft (`R3.TOP_WIDE` and `R3.SHOW_MIN` in `mocks/welcome/r4-kit.js`), and a soft frame is centred on the photo. `mock-qa/wide-check.mjs` now includes 3440 x 1230. Round 3's `extend()` takes `settle` as a default argument, fixed when the function is defined, so setting the module's `SETTLE` did nothing, and at this photo's softness its 768 px blurs took most of an hour. `prep-welcome-r4.py` passes `settle` on each call and blurs big sigmas at a reduced scale, in 53 s.

## Gotchas

- `npm run lint` reads `mocks/` locally and fails on vendor files there; CI never sees them. Never import from `mocks/` or `scripts-local/` in committed code.
- `file://` pages aren't a secure context, so the clipboard is blocked; serve them. Windows paths into WSL can show a stale cached copy.
- Pick a free port; other sessions leave servers running.
- `scripts/photos/open.mjs` (`openCommand`) opens a file in his Windows browser from WSL, and `explorer.exe <file>` does too, exiting 1 even when it works. Don't use them to hand him something: give the `http://localhost` link and the Windows path instead ("stop opening the file explorer everytime", his rule for every repo).
- Playwright's cached Chromium in WSL won't start without `libnspr4`, `libnss3` and `libasound2t64`. Without sudo, `apt-get download` them, `dpkg-deb -x` each into a folder and point `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` at its `usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`.
- That headless Chromium never paints the next page after a cross-document view transition (even two bare pages with `@view-transition { navigation: auto }`), so screenshots and clicks time out. Check page changes in VS Code's integrated browser (`openBrowserPage`, `runPlaywrightCode`, reading `pagereveal`'s `viewTransition`), and run headless checks with `reducedMotion: 'reduce'`.
- Same-document view transitions (`document.startViewTransition`) do run in headless Chromium, and Playwright can screenshot mid-transition, unlike cross-document ones. To mock a page change, put the pages in one document, swap them inside the callback, and use the same `view-transition-name` CSS the real cross-document change would. A `--slow` multiplier on every duration lets him watch it at ×4.
- Live content for a mock: `scripts-local/prep-portfolio.mjs` reads trumanbrown.com's home and Things to try pages and saves the covers, lead frames, rail, places and plates into the mock folder. `mocks/portfolio/lib.js` is the real `globe.ts` and `motion.ts` bundled with esbuild from `_lib.ts`.
- Check every mock the same way with `scripts-local/mock-qa/` (setup in its README): `welcome-qa.sh` takes screenshots at desktop and phone width in both themes and runs axe, Impeccable's detector (tiny text, text under other things, overflow, hidden content) and Lighthouse, and `welcome-film.mjs` films an interaction from the browser's own frames into a timed strip. Impeccable runs locally and signed out, but never run its `install` or Live mode, which can start agents outside approval.
- Film each entrance from the first paint, in both themes. The welcome columns mock held its columns almost invisible while their photos decoded, so its dark page background showed for about 80ms on a light page (2026-11-19). Impeccable's contrast check reads text against the nearest parent with a background colour, never the photo under it, so changing a page background can flip its verdict either way.
- An `<img>` with `srcset` and `sizes` but no size of its own paints at the `sizes` width before a script places it, which counts as layout shift. Hide such layers until they're placed, and place them at DOMContentLoaded (`.r3-scene.placed` in `mocks/welcome/r3-kit.css`).
- Creating a WebGL context takes 300 to 400 ms in WSL's software renderer and blocks the page. Make it after the entrance, on idle, and keep the depth motion off until its first frame is drawn: before that the flat photo still holds him, so moving it would ghost his outline.
- `composite: "add"` on an opacity keyframe adds to the element's own opacity, so an entrance with a delay shows at full strength through the delay. Animate the transform with `add` and the opacity separately with the default `replace`.
- A small thing moving on a full-screen canvas under frosted glass costs the whole page. Every time the canvas changes, every `backdrop-filter` element above it redraws. Round 3's eagle dropped E, the direction with the most glass, to 651 of 720 frames at 120 Hz. The kit was also redrawing its full-screen depth plate every frame while only the eagle moved. A small canvas that travels with the eagle by `transform`, and no plate redraw while the spring is at rest, brought every page back to 720 of 720. Compare with the part switched off on the real GPU (`mock-qa/raf-gaps.mjs`, `bird=0`).
- A small label laid over the scene (round 3's `R3.where`) has to be placed after the page's controls have finished coming in, so the kit waits for every running animation to end (`document.getAnimations()`) and places it again. Measure a name by its text nodes (`Range.getClientRects`), not its element: a centred name's element box spans the whole width. Keep it off his outline with `S.spans(y)`, and pick its colour from the photo's brightness under it, the same map the glass reads.
- A drift slower than about 5 px a second on soft cirrus is invisible, even though the shader runs. A difference image between two moments of a film shows what moved (`mock-qa/cloud-diff.py`, and `mock-qa/cloud-probe.mjs` with `TUNE` to try a speed). The round 3 clouds run at about 7 px a second.
- `python3 -m http.server` sends no cache headers, so after a fix the browser can paint yesterday's images from its cache for an hour or more. The round 3 pages load the kit as `r3-kit.js?v=<date>` and the kit adds the same `?v` to the layers it loads (`R3.V`). Bump both whenever the layers or the kit change, or ask for a hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R).
- `mocks/welcome/mock.js` already reads `photo` from the URL (the hero photo in rounds 1 and 2). A round's own switch needs a key it doesn't use: round 3's Photographs picture is `pic`.
- Every count on a door carries its unit ("6 hobbies", "5 roles"). A bare "7" confused a reviewer in welcome round 1, and two round 2 builders still wrote bare counts from `S.hobbies.length`, which also counts Narrow nature. Put the wording in the brief.
- A motion change on a live toy: `scripts-local/prep-satisfying.mjs` saves live pages with their compiled CSS and no scripts as `live.html`. Each mock bundles the island's real script as `today.js` and a changed copy of its engine as `new.js` (`npx --yes esbuild <entry> --bundle --format=iife`), and `mocks/satisfying/frame.js` shows the page at desktop and phone width with Today and Proposed, theme, reduced motion and Slow ×4 switches (`_live/boot.js` reads them from the URL). Truman can compare the real thing with the change without anything ported. Two catches: the live site's files are same-site only, so anything a toy fetches at runtime (Narrow nature's relief tiles) needs a local copy or a symlink into `public/`, and Vite's `import.meta.glob` doesn't bundle with plain esbuild (`mocks/satisfying/narrow-nature/_src/build.mjs` swaps it out).

Add new verdicts and lessons here, dated, in the commit that acts on them.
